clinicalPearls: A proliferative retinal vascular disorder affecting premature, low-birthweight infants, and a leading preventable cause of childhood blindness
The principal risk factors are low gestational age, low birthweight, and prolonged or unregulated supplemental oxygen exposure
Screening of at-risk preterm infants according to gestational age and birthweight thresholds is essential because early disease is asymptomatic

Severity is described by zone (I to III, indicating how posterior the disease is), stage (1 to 5, from a demarcation line to total retinal detachment), and the presence of 'plus' disease (dilated, tortuous posterior vessels)
'Plus' disease and posterior (zone I) involvement are the key markers of aggressive disease needing treatment
Treatment of threshold or type 1 disease is with laser ablation of the avascular peripheral retina, with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy used in selected cases
Advanced untreated disease progresses to tractional retinal detachment (stages 4 and 5) with severe visual loss
Survivors remain at increased lifelong risk of myopia, strabismus, amblyopia, and late retinal detachment, requiring ongoing follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Retinopathy of prematurity results from disordered development of the retinal vasculature in the incompletely vascularised preterm retina. In an initial phase, the relatively hyperoxic extrauterine environment (worsened by supplemental oxygen) suppresses vascular growth factors and halts normal vessel growth, leaving peripheral avascular retina. As the metabolically active retina matures, the resulting hypoxia drives excessive vascular endothelial growth factor production and pathological neovascularisation at the junction of vascular and avascular retina. These new vessels can bleed and form fibrovascular tissue, exerting traction that leads to retinal detachment.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous)
Congenital retinal fold or other developmental vitreoretinopathies
additionalInvestigations: Structured screening dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy of at-risk preterm infants at defined intervals
Documentation of zone, stage, and presence of plus disease at each examination
Wide-field retinal imaging where available to aid documentation and telemedicine review
Longer-term assessment of refraction, ocular alignment, and amblyopia in survivors
redFlags: Zone I disease or the presence of plus disease indicating aggressive, treatment-requiring retinopathy
Rapidly progressive posterior (aggressive) ROP that can advance to detachment quickly
Any signs of tractional retinal detachment (stage 4 or 5)
Missed or delayed screening in eligible infants, risking preventable blindness
reference.prognosis: Mild ROP frequently regresses spontaneously with a good visual outcome, but severe disease can progress to retinal detachment and blindness if untreated. Timely screening and treatment markedly reduce the risk of severe visual loss, though treated eyes and preterm survivors remain prone to refractive error, strabismus, and amblyopia.
pitfalls: Failing to screen eligible preterm infants or examining them too late to intervene
Underestimating aggressive posterior disease that lacks the classic ridge appearance
Poor regulation of supplemental oxygen increasing the risk and severity of disease
Discharging treated infants without long-term follow-up for refractive and detachment risks
management: Ablate the avascular peripheral retina with laser photocoagulation for type 1 (threshold) disease to halt the neovascular drive
Reserve intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy (such as bevacizumab or ranibizumab) for aggressive posterior or zone I disease, with vigilant follow-up for reactivation
Regulate supplemental oxygen to targeted saturation ranges and avoid unnecessary hyperoxia to limit ongoing vascular injury
Enrol at-risk preterm infants in structured screening dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy at intervals set by gestational age and birthweight
Refer for vitreoretinal surgery (scleral buckling or vitrectomy) when tractional retinal detachment develops
Provide long-term surveillance for refractive error, strabismus and amblyopia in treated eyes and preterm survivors
Coordinate care between neonatology and ophthalmology and counsel parents on the visual prognosis
